content: The co-occurrence of HIV and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) presents significant challenges in clinical management, including limited treatment options and poorer treatment outcomes. Population-level data on the relationship between HIV and MDR-TB remain scarce, partly because only 40% of individuals with active TB are tested for HIV. Documented outbreaks of MDR-TB among people living with HIV have been reported in hospitals and other settings, particularly in Eastern Europe and Southern African countries with high HIV prevalence. For individuals with HIV suspected of having drug-resistant TB, the use of the Xpert MTB/RIF diagnostic test is recommended where available. This test is more sensitive in detecting TB among people with HIV and can rapidly identify rifampicin resistance, significantly reducing the time to diagnosis and initiation of MDR-TB treatment. Efforts to reduce the burden of MDR-TB should focus on strengthening HIV prevention, improving infection control, and enhancing collaboration between HIV and TB control programs. Special attention should be given to high-risk groups, such as people who inject drugs and those exposed in congregate settings. Cryptococcal meningitis is a critical opportunistic infection and a major cause of mortality both before and after the initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART). The World Health Organization (WHO) 2011 Rapid Advice provides guidance on the diagnosis, screening, prevention, and management of cryptococcal infection, including induction, consolidation, and maintenance treatment regimens, as well as monitoring and managing toxicities. ART initiation in patients with cryptococcal meningitis should be delayed until there is evidence of a sustained clinical response to antifungal therapy, typically after 2–4 weeks of induction and consolidation treatment with amphotericin-based regimens or 4–6 weeks of high-dose oral fluconazole. Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection affects 5–20% of the 33 million people living with HIV globally, while hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection affects 5–15%, with rates as high as 90% among people who inject drugs. The burden of coinfection is highest in lowand middle-income countries, particularly in Southeast Asia and sub-Saharan Africa for HBV. Viral hepatitis is an increasing cause of morbidity and mortality among people living with HIV, including those on ART. A comprehensive approach to managing HBV and HCV coinfection includes prevention, screening, vaccination, and treatment. WHO guidelines for managing hepatitis C are expected to provide detailed recommendations on screening, treatment, and care. Malaria poses a significant risk to people living with HIV, particularly those with immunosuppression in malaria-endemic areas. Infants, children under five, and pregnant women are at particular risk of severe malaria and its complications. Key interventions include prompt and effective treatment with artemisinin-based combination therapies, the use of insecticide-treated nets, and indoor residual spraying. In areas of high malaria transmission, intermittent preventive treatment during pregnancy and seasonal malaria chemoprophylaxis are recommended for high-risk groups. People living with HIV who develop malaria should receive effective antimalarial treatment promptly, with parasitological confirmation of diagnosis. Drug interactions and shared toxicities between antimalarial and antiretroviral drugs should be closely monitored. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) frequently coexist with HIV and can enhance HIV transmission. Many STIs are asymptomatic, particularly in women, but can still cause complications and be transmitted to sexual partners. HIV alters the natural history of STIs, increasing the risk of complications. Routine screening, diagnosis, and treatment of STIs should be integrated into comprehensive HIV care. Women living with HIV are at higher risk of pre-cancerous and invasive cervical cancer due to persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, which is exacerbated by low CD4 counts and high HIV viral loads. Cervical cancer screening and early management of pre-cancerous lesions are essential for all women living with HIV, regardless of ART status or age. Vaccination is critical for people living with HIV, who should receive all routine vaccines according to national immunization schedules. Live vaccines may pose risks for those with severe immunosuppression, while inactivated vaccines are generally safe and effective, particularly for individuals on ART. Comprehensive vaccination strategies should be implemented to protect this population. People living with HIV are at increased risk of developing noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic lung disease, and certain cancers. Effective ART has extended the lifespan of people with HIV, leading to a higher prevalence of age-related NCDs. Integrating NCD screening and management into chronic HIV care, including interventions like dietary counseling, smoking cessation, and blood pressure monitoring, can reduce NCD risks. WHO has developed a package of essential NCD interventions for primary care in low-resource settings. Mental health conditions, including depression, anxiety, dementia, and substance use disorders, are common among people living with HIV and can impact ART adherence and retention in care. HIV care settings provide an opportunity to detect and manage mental health disorders. WHO’s Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP) offers general mental health recommendations relevant to people living with HIV, with additional guidance on mental health management planned. People living with HIV who use drugs face a range of challenges, including drug dependence, withdrawal, and overdose, as well as bloodborne infections like viral hepatitis and bacterial endocarditis. WHO has developed guidance for the treatment of opioid dependence and related conditions.
